title: Frontend Engineering
tagline: Modern web interfaces, performance budgets, accessibility, and client architecture
description: A complete path from semantic HTML and modern CSS through JavaScript/TypeScript internals, modern component architecture, state management, and web performance optimization.
prerequisites: Understanding of how the web works

stages.title: Stage 1: Web Foundations & Accessibility
stages.description: Master document structure, semantic markup, accessible landmarks, and intrinsic responsive layouts.

nodes.title: Semantic HTML & Accessibility Landmarks
nodes.description: Structured markup using meaningful elements (<main>, <nav>, <article>, <header>, <section>) rather than generic div containers.
nodes.whyItMatters: Accessibility assistive tech (screen readers) and search engines navigate through the accessibility tree. Semantic structure drastically reduces custom ARIA hacks and improves indexability.
keyTakeaways: Use native interactive elements (<button>, <a href>, <dialog>) to get built-in keyboard navigation and focus management.
Maintain strict heading levels (h1 through h6) without skipping levels.
Verify all interactive elements provide visible text or descriptive aria-label.
nodes.interviewTips: Expect questions contrasting <div> vs semantic elements, and how browser accessibility trees are constructed from the DOM.

nodes.title: Modern CSS: Grid, Flexbox & Container Queries
nodes.description: Layout systems for one-dimensional alignments (Flexbox), two-dimensional grids (CSS Grid), and modular container queries.
nodes.whyItMatters: Fluid, responsive CSS prevents brittle breakpoint media queries, eliminates Cumulative Layout Shifts (CLS), and ensures interfaces adapt to any viewport or card width.
keyTakeaways: Use Flexbox for unidirectional flow and toolbar items; use CSS Grid for page skeleton layouts.
Container queries enable reusable components that respond to their container width rather than global screen dimensions.
Leverage minmax(), clamp(), and calc() to create scalable fluid typography.
nodes.interviewTips: Common questions include CSS specificity calculations, margin collapsing rules, and building responsive card grids without media queries.

nodes.title: Browser Architecture & DOM Manipulation
nodes.description: Understanding the Critical Rendering Path: parsing HTML/CSS, DOM and CSSOM generation, render tree, layout/reflow, paint, and compositing.
nodes.whyItMatters: Frequent DOM writes and layout thrashing drop animation framerates below 60fps. Understanding the rendering pipeline is key to smooth UI performance.
keyTakeaways: Avoid reading computed layout properties immediately after writing styles to prevent forced synchronous layouts.
Prefer CSS transforms and opacity for animations because they run on the GPU compositor thread.
Understand event bubbling, capturing, and delegation to optimize memory usage.
nodes.interviewTips: Be prepared to explain the exact steps a browser takes from entering a URL to displaying pixels on the screen.

stages.title: Stage 2: JavaScript Runtime & TypeScript
stages.description: Deep dive into execution context, event loop, asynchronous promises, closures, and static type safety.

nodes.title: Async JS & The Event Loop
nodes.description: Call stack, Web APIs, Microtask queue (Promises), Macrotask queue (setTimeout, I/O), and event loop ticks.
nodes.whyItMatters: JavaScript is single-threaded. Blocking the call stack freezes user input, drops frames, and triggers 'Page Unresponsive' warnings.

resources.title: Philip Roberts: What the heck is the event loop anyway?

keyTakeaways: Microtasks (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) run immediately after the current script and before any macrotasks.
Use AbortController to cleanly cancel fetch requests and prevent memory leaks or stale state race conditions.
Always handle Promise rejections to prevent unhandled rejection crashes.
nodes.interviewTips: Almost every senior frontend interview includes predicting output order for mixed setTimeout, Promise.then, and console.log snippets.

nodes.title: TypeScript in Modern Applications
nodes.description: Static type system: generics, union types, discriminated unions, utility types, and strict mode.
nodes.whyItMatters: Catches entire classes of runtime null/undefined bugs at compile time and makes large codebases refactorable with confidence.
keyTakeaways: Use discriminated unions to represent distinct UI states (idle, loading, success, error) safely.
Enable strict: true in tsconfig to enforce null checks and avoid implicit any types.
Favor interfaces/types with readonly attributes for immutable state models.
nodes.interviewTips: Expect questions on generics, `keyof`, `typeof`, type narrowing via type guards, and `unknown` vs `any`.

stages.title: Stage 3: Modern UI Architecture & State
stages.description: Component design systems, declarative rendering, state management patterns, and client-server synchronization.

nodes.title: Component Design Systems & Composition
nodes.description: Building composable, accessible UI libraries with clear props contracts, slots/children composition, and design tokens.
nodes.whyItMatters: Duplicated ad-hoc UI code creates visual inconsistencies, accessibility regressions, and engineering velocity bottlenecks.
keyTakeaways: Prefer composition over deep prop-drilling or giant multi-boolean configurations.
Separate presentational dumb components from stateful container components.
Use design tokens (colors, spacing, shadows) defined once in CSS variables.
nodes.interviewTips: You may be asked to design an accessible Modal, Dropdown, or Combobox component from scratch with keyboard focus trap.

nodes.title: Client State vs Server Cache
nodes.description: Differentiating transient local UI state from remote server cache (TanStack Query, SWR, Zustand).
nodes.whyItMatters: Overusing global Redux stores for server data leads to stale cache bugs, duplicate fetch calls, and painful manual cache invalidation.
keyTakeaways: Server state is owned by the backend and cached on the client; UI state is ephemeral and purely client-side.
Use automatic query deduplication, optimistic updates, and background revalidation.
Keep state as close to the consuming component as possible.
nodes.interviewTips: Interviewers often test your knowledge of caching strategies: stale-while-revalidate, optimistic updates, and cache invalidation.

stages.title: Stage 4: Web Vitals & Production Performance
stages.description: Real-world web performance: LCP, INP, CLS, code-splitting, asset delivery, and bundle analysis.

nodes.title: Core Web Vitals & Loading Optimization
nodes.description: Mastering Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).
nodes.whyItMatters: Every 100ms of latency costs e-commerce conversion. Google search rankings penalize slow CWV metrics.
keyTakeaways: Optimize LCP by prioritizing the hero image with fetchpriority='high' and preloading critical web fonts.
Prevent CLS by explicitly declaring width and height attributes on images and video placeholders.
Keep long tasks under 50ms using scheduler.yield() or web workers to achieve excellent INP (<200ms).
nodes.interviewTips: Be prepared to explain how to diagnose slow LCP in Chrome DevTools and the architectural fixes required.

nodes.title: Frontend Security: XSS, CSRF & CSP
nodes.description: Preventing Cross-Site Scripting, securing cookies with HttpOnly and SameSite, and crafting strict Content Security Policies.
nodes.whyItMatters: One unescaped innerHTML call can allow attackers to steal user session tokens and take over accounts.

resources.title: OWASP Top Ten Web Application Security

keyTakeaways: Never inject untrusted user input directly into innerHTML or dangerouslySetInnerHTML without DOMPurify sanitization.
Store authentication session cookies with HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite=Lax flags.
Deploy a strict CSP header disallowing unsafe-eval and unauthorized remote script origins.
nodes.interviewTips: Expect questions on how XSS differs from CSRF, and how modern frameworks prevent XSS by default via text node escaping.
